newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico ends corruption probe of scandal-hit agency.
newsitem.headline: Mexico ends corruption probe of scandal-hit agency.

text.p: Amid charges of a cover-up, a ruling party-led Congressional commission on Wednesday ended its investigation into troubled food subsidy agency Conasupo that had involved allegations against President Ernesto Zedillo.

Opposition congressmen stormed out of a meeting announcing the closure of the probe, accusing the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) of a whitewash that some alleged was ordered by Zedillo's government.
"They made a pantomime of work," said Javier Gutierrez of the opposition National Action Party.

The commission's findings included evidence of irregularities between 1982 and 1992 but news reports said it played down some high-profile cases including those involving Raul Salinas, a former head of Conasupo who is ex-President Carlos Salinas' brother.
Raul Salinas is currently in jail on murder and embezzlement charges.
The commission recommended five suspects be brought to trial, none of whom was a high-ranking member of the government-run agency, Notimex added.

"It's been a formal, serious commission. If they don't like the results that's not our fault," the commission's president told a news conference. His party, the PRI, has ruled Mexico for 67 years, always with a huge majority in Congress.

The commission was racked by controversy in July when an independent congressman and commission member, Adolfo Aguilar Zinser, charged that Zedillo was linked to a questionable $7 million payment by Conasupo to its supplier Maseca, a top corn flour company.
But the commission's leaders ruled that there was no evidence of wrongdoing and it stopped the investigation.
Zinser, who called the commission a cover-up, alleged that Zedillo's government had ordered it stopped.

"The investigation that I carried out on the Maseca case that involved the then Minister of Budget and Planning (Zedillo) ... was considered an affront that meant the commission was closed down," he told Reuters.
